title: Tool Dependency Graph
summary_easy: AI agents often fail because a tool needs an ID that only another tool can provide, like the thread ID needed to reply to an email. Tanay built a system that reads the schemas of 1,391 tools and maps which tools must run first and which inputs must come from the user. About two thirds of required inputs turn out to be handles another tool can supply, and almost all of those have a producer.
summary_deep: A TypeScript and Bun static analyser over a production catalog of 1,391 tools (896 GitHub, the rest a Google suite). JSON Schemas are flattened into leaf slots with paths and compounding requiredness; Google tools get a service by weighted regex markers with a confidence floor. Input slots resolve to one of 46 namespaced, service scoped entities or fall into user supplied, control, enum, or reported unresolved buckets; outputs resolve in three tiers (leaf, nearest meaningful ancestor, owning slug) so threads[].id becomes gmail.thread_id. Producers are primary when the head noun of the slug's object phrase names the entity, incidental ones are suppressed, and a hand weighted score ranks the rest within the toolkit. The graph is bipartite (tools and entities both nodes, 3,278 edges) with one hop plans per tool. Of 2,728 required inputs, 1,770 resolve to an entity and 1,768 of those have a producer; the slug fallback fired zero times. Validation is eight hand written assertions; no labelled precision or recall and no transitive planner exist yet.

sheet.easy:
## What it is
A map, built only from tool schemas, of which agent tools must run before which, and which inputs must come from the user.

## Why
A reply tool needs a thread ID. Nobody knows it by heart; an earlier call has to return it. Without the map, agents invent IDs or ask users for things users cannot know.

## Headline numbers
| | |
|---|---|
| Tools | 1,391 (GitHub and a Google suite) |
| Typed entities | 46 |
| Edges | 3,278 |
| Required inputs | 2,728 |
| Resolved to an entity | 1,770 (65%) |
| Of those, with a producer | 1,768 (99.9%) |
| Handle shaped, not yet covered | 568 |
| Slug guessing fallback used | 0 times |

Read 99.9% carefully: it covers only the inputs that resolved to an entity.

## Three ideas
1. **Namespaced entities.** `id` on a mail tool can only mean a mail thing, so mail never gets wired to GitHub.
2. **Read the path.** `threads[].id` is a thread ID; the meaning is in the parent.
3. **Head noun.** CREATE_A_REPOSITORY_VARIABLE makes a variable, not a repo.

## Why bipartite
Tools and entities are both nodes. One entity, the repo owner, would otherwise create tens of thousands of tool to tool arrows.

## Checks
Eight hand written assertions; all started failing; four caught real bugs. A spot check, not an evaluation.

## Not built yet
Multi step plans (topological order), a labelled precision and recall set, automatic registry growth.
sheet.deep:
## Pipeline
1. `normalizeTool` (src/extract.ts): probe field spellings, flatten input and output schemas into slots.
2. `inferService` (src/entities.ts): GitHub by toolkit; Google suite by weighted markers, floor 3, else `google_other`.
3. `classifySlot`: entity, enum, control, user supplied, handle shaped unresolved, default user supplied.
4. `resolveEntityFromContext` for outputs: leaf, nearest non envelope ancestor, owning slug.
5. Produces with depth and `primary`; slug fallback only when outputs are empty (fired 0 times).
6. Bipartite edges: tool to entity (produces), entity to tool (requires, with `required` flag).
7. Plans: candidates minus self, primary filter, local toolkit filter, `producerScore`, sort, cap 12; `askUser`.
8. `viz.ts`: slim and inline into graph.html (Cytoscape, cose layout, 260 node cap per service).

## Flattening rules
- Paths: `a.b`, arrays of objects add `[]` and set `repeated`; arrays of scalars are slots.
- `required(child) = required(parent) AND key in parent.required` (compounding).
- `$ref` local only (`#/...`), `activeRefs` guard per branch; combinators collapse to first structural branch.
- `MAX_DEPTH = 7`. Envelope keys stripped for `coreFieldPath`: data, response_data, result, items, records.

## Service score
$$\text{score}(s)=\sum_{m\in M_s} w_m\,(3[\text{params}]+3[\text{defs}]+2[\text{slug}]+1[\text{desc}])$$
Assign argmax if score at least 3. Breakdown: github 896, google_other 112, googledrive 96, googlesheets 62, gmail 54, googledocs 39, googlecalendar 36, googleads 28, googleanalytics 26, googletasks 18, googlephotos 11, googlemaps 9, googlecontacts 4.

## Slot buckets
| bucket | rule |
|---|---|
| tool_derived | alias hit for an in scope entity (service scoped beats `*`) |
| enum_or_constant | schema has `enum` |
| control | page, per_page, cursor, limit, sort, format, fields, filter, state, user_id, auth tokens, ... |
| user_supplied | subject, body, text, title, query, name, dates, url, ... or default |
| unresolved | `(^|_)(id|ids|number|sha|token|slug|key|uri|resource_name)$` with no entity |

## Three tier output resolution
1. leaf alias; 2. if leaf in {id, ids, number, key, slug, value}: walk ancestors, skip envelope segments, first entity whose object nouns match (singular or plural); 3. first entity implied by the owner slug.

## Primary producer (head noun)
Object phrase = tokens after first verb in {LIST, SEARCH, GET, FETCH, FIND, CREATE} up to first preposition, minus articles. Primary iff last token (or joined phrase, or last two joined) is an object noun of the entity.

## Producer score
$$50[\text{schema}]+70[\text{same service}]+30[\text{same toolkit}]+100[\text{primary}]+30[\text{read}]+40[\text{head hit}]-12\max(0,d-1)-\min(24,2\,n_{tok})+8[\_LIST\_]+6[\_SEARCH\_]$$
Sort descending, tie by slug, keep 12.

## Edge counts
Direct: $\sum_e p_e c_e$ (repo_owner alone: $146\times637$, about 93,000). Bipartite: $\sum_e (p_e+c_e)=3{,}278$.

## Results (data/graph.json stats, README)
| metric | value |
|---|---|
| tools | 1,391 |
| entities | 46 |
| edges | 3,278 |
| input slots | 7,101 (2,728 required) |
| required resolved to entity | 1,770 of 2,728 (65%) |
| with at least one producer | 1,768 of 1,770 (99.9%) |
| tools with real output schema | 1,238 of 1,391 (89%) |
| slug inference used | 0 |
| unresolved handle slots | 568 |

Uncovered required entity slots: GET_ATTACHMENT attachment_id (gmail.attachment_id), ADD_SUB_ISSUE issue_id (github.issue_id).

## check.py (8 assertions)
Reply needs thread id; LIST_THREADS supplies it; send mail resolves email; a contacts tool supplies it; no GitHub tool in a Gmail plan; optional attachment fields not required; issue comment needs issue number; an issue LIST, GET or SEARCH tool supplies it. Bugs found: bare id under threads[], cross service leak, requiredness not compounding, head noun.

## Planning (not built)
AND/OR graph: tool needs all required entities; entity needs any producer or the user. Forward chaining fixpoint with unmet counters, $O(V+E)$, cycle safe. Kahn's algorithm for plain DAGs: in degree queue, $O(V+E)$, leftover nodes mean a cycle.

## Evaluation (not built)
Stratified hand labelled consumers; precision@1, @3; recall of producers; slot recall; per service; two labellers; end to end agent success with and without hints.

## Known errors to fix
repo_name precursors are incidental (listings call it `name`); tier 2 first match maps issues[].id to issue_number; 153 tools with no informative output schema; first branch combinator collapse; depth 7.

## Glossary
JSON Schema, `$ref`, `$defs`, anyOf, oneOf, allOf, slot, entity, alias, object noun, opaque handle, semi opaque, service scoping, envelope, primary and incidental producer, head final compound, bipartite graph, hub, degree, two hop path, precursor, askUser, topological sort, Kahn's algorithm, AND/OR graph, forward chaining, Cytoscape, cose layout.

narration.script:
The problem is boring and common. A reply tool needs a thread ID, and nobody has one memorised. It only exists because some earlier call returned it. An agent that doesn't know that either invents an ID or asks the user for something the user can't know.

So I built a map from nothing but JSON Schemas. The catalog has 1,391 tools across GitHub and a Google suite. I flatten every input and output schema into leaf fields with paths, and I make requiredness compound down the tree, so a field inside an optional attachment isn't required.

The obvious version matches input names to output names. It fails three ways. Generic names like id collide everywhere, so I resolve handles to namespaced entities scoped to the owning service. A bare id means nothing, so for a field like threads[].id I read the parent segment, then the tool's own object. And almost every response embeds other objects, so I mark a producer primary only when the head noun of its slug names the entity. CREATE_A_REPOSITORY_VARIABLE makes a variable, not a repo.

Tools and entities are both nodes, so the graph stays readable. The repo owner entity alone would otherwise generate tens of thousands of edges.

Results: 65% of required inputs are typed handles, and of those, 1,768 out of 1,770 have a producer. A slug guessing fallback fired zero times, so every edge cites a declared output field. Eight hand written assertions pass, and four of them caught real bugs.

What's missing: a labelled set for precision and recall, and a planner that chains the one hop answers into a full call order. Those are next.

narration.prompt: Give me the full technical story, as if I were a staff engineer.
narration.script:
The input is a catalog of 1,391 tools, each with an input and output JSON Schema. 896 are GitHub. The rest are a Google suite that flattens Gmail, Drive, Calendar, Sheets and others under one prefix.

Step one is flattening. A recursive walker resolves local refs with a guard against recursive schemas, collapses anyOf and oneOf onto the first branch with structure, and emits leaves with dotted paths, array markers, and a repeated flag. Requiredness compounds: a field is required only if every ancestor is. That was a real bug, because fields inside an optional attachment were showing up as required user input.

Step two is service inference for the Google suite. Slugs alone can't tell Gmail labels from Drive labels from Ads labels. So each service has weighted regex markers, matched against parameter names and output type names at triple weight, the slug at double, and the description once. Below a floor of 3 the tool is parked in google_other instead of guessed.

Step three is the entity registry: 46 namespaced entities with aliases, object nouns, scope, and an opaque flag. Input slots resolve to an entity inside the owning service, then fall into enum, control, user supplied, or an unresolved bucket for handle shaped names nothing covers. That bucket is reported, and it's where several entities came from.

Step four is output resolution, in three tiers. First the leaf name. If the leaf is generic, like id, walk up to the nearest non envelope ancestor, so threads[].id becomes a Gmail thread. Failing that, use the tool's own object from its slug.

Step five is deciding which producers matter. A workflow run response embeds a whole repository, so literally it produces a repo name. I parse the slug: first verb, then the object phrase up to the first preposition, articles dropped. English compounds are head final, so the last noun is the object. A tool is a primary producer only if that head noun names the entity. In plans, incidental producers are dropped whenever a primary exists. Then I keep producers in the same toolkit if any exist, score them, and keep twelve. The score adds points for schema evidence, locality, purpose, read verbs, and the head match, and subtracts for depth and long slugs.

The graph is bipartite. Repo owner has 146 producers and 637 consumers, so a direct encoding would put roughly 93,000 edges on that one entity. With entities as nodes the total is 3,278.

Results with denominators. 7,101 input slots, 2,728 required. 65% of the required ones resolve to an entity, and 1,768 of those 1,770 have a producer. The two misses are a Gmail attachment ID and a GitHub issue's global ID. The slug fallback fired zero times.

Now the weak spots, before you find them. There's no labelled set, so no precision or recall. Eight assertions are a spot check. Looking at the plans, the repo name precursors for commenting on an issue are incidental tools, because repository listings call the field name, which no alias catches. And I think tier two's first match rule maps an issue's global id to issue number, which would explain why issue_id has no producer. Finally, it only answers one hop. A real planner is an AND/OR problem: a tool needs all its inputs, an input needs any producer. Forward chaining to a fixpoint handles that in linear time and is cycle safe. That's the next thing I'd build, along with a labelled sample.

Flattening details and the requiredness bug
Weighted service inference with a floor
Registry, slot buckets, unresolved as backlog
Head noun primary producers, locality, score
Volunteers gaps: no eval, repo_name noise, issue_id, one hop only

About two thirds of the required inputs turn out to be things another tool can supply. I also wrote down the cases I cared about in advance and checked the map against them, which caught four real mistakes.

narration.prompt: How exactly do you resolve a bare id in an output?
narration.script: In three tiers, widest context last. First I try the leaf name against the registry, scoped to the tool's service. If the leaf is generic, like id or number, I walk up the path, skip envelope segments like data and items, and take the first meaningful ancestor. So threads[].id becomes a Gmail thread ID. If every ancestor is envelope, I use the tool's own object from its slug, so LIST_REPOSITORY_ISSUES with items[].number yields an issue. If none of that works, I return nothing rather than guess. One weakness: tier two takes the first registry match, which can pick issue number where issue global id was meant.
keypoints: Leaf, then ancestor, then slug object

narration.prompt: How do you choose which producer to suggest?
narration.script: Two filters, then a score. If any producer is primary, meaning the head noun of its slug names the entity, I drop the incidental ones. If any producer is in the same toolkit, I drop the rest. Then I score what's left: points for coming from a real schema, same service, same toolkit, being primary, being a read tool, and the head noun match. I subtract for how deep the field sits in the response and for long, narrow slugs. Ties break alphabetically, and I keep twelve. The weights are hand set, so I'd fit them on labelled data once I have it.
keypoints: Weights are hand set, would fit with labels

narration.prompt: How would you turn this into a full call order? Is it a topological sort?
narration.script: Not quite. A topological sort assumes every predecessor must run. Here a tool needs all of its required inputs, but each input can come from any one of several producers, or from the user. That's an AND/OR graph. I'd start from what the user already knows, keep a counter of unmet inputs per tool, and fire a tool when its counter hits zero, marking its outputs available. That runs to a fixpoint in linear time and can't loop, because each node flips once. Then I'd walk back from the goal, picking the best scored producer for each missing input.

narration.prompt: How would you measure precision and recall?
narration.script: I'd build a labelled sample, because right now there isn't one. I'd pick about a hundred consuming tools, stratified by service and by how busy their entities are. For each required handle, a person writes down the acceptable producers. Precision at one and at three tells me whether the first suggestions are usable, since an agent tries the first one. Recall tells me whether the true producers appear at all. I'd report it per service, have a second labeller do a subset for agreement, and turn every error into an assertion in the check script.

narration.prompt: 99.9% coverage sounds like a vanity number.
narration.script: It's easy to misread, so I put the denominator next to it. It's coverage of the 1,770 required inputs that resolved to an entity, out of 2,728 required in total. The honest figure is that 65% of required inputs are typed handles, and almost all of those have a producer. It also doesn't say the top suggestion is correct. I can show you a precursor list for repo name that's mostly incidental tools. Precision needs a labelled sample, which is my next step. What I can stand behind is that every edge cites a declared output field.

narration.prompt: Models can figure out tool order themselves. Why build a static graph?
narration.script: On a small toolset, a strong model usually gets it right, and I won't argue otherwise. At 1,391 tools the output schemas don't fit in context, and output schemas are what tell you who produces a handle. A guessed ID fails late and confusingly, often after the agent has already acted. The graph is deterministic, costs nothing at runtime, and every edge is auditable. It's meant to work alongside the model. The graph proposes a short list of precursors and what to ask the user, and the model decides with the runtime context the graph doesn't have.

cards.q: Why does this matter for agents?
cards.easy: Agents often fail a tool call because it needs an argument they cannot produce. A reply tool needs a thread ID, which nobody knows by heart; it only exists because an earlier call returned it. Without a map of that ordering, the agent either makes up the ID or asks the user for something the user cannot know either.
cards.deep: The failure mode is an unsatisfiable argument, not a reasoning error. Opaque handles (thread ids, issue numbers, commit shas, spreadsheet ids) must come from a prior call; semi opaque values such as an email address may come from the user or from a lookup; freeform content (subject, body) must come from the user. A model given only tool descriptions has to infer that structure every time, and tends to hallucinate plausible looking ids. A precomputed dependency map turns that into a lookup: for REPLY_TO_THREAD, the precursor for gmail.thread_id is LIST_THREADS (or a message listing), and the only thing to ask the user for is the body. It also feeds tool retrieval and planning: if a tool is selected, its precursors can be pulled into context too.

cards.q: Define the JSON Schema features this parser has to handle.
cards.easy: JSON Schema describes the shape of a JSON document: which fields an object has, which are required, what type each is, and what an array contains. Larger schemas reuse definitions by reference and combine alternatives.
cards.deep: type (string, or a list such as ["string", "null"]; typeOf drops null and joins the rest); properties (map of field name to subschema); required (list of field names required at that level only, which is why requiredness must compound down the tree); items (subschema for array elements; an array of objects becomes a path segment with [], an array of scalars is itself the slot); enum (fixed vocabulary, classified enum_or_constant); default (recorded as hasDefault); $ref with $defs or definitions (local references like #/$defs/Thread, resolved against the document root); anyOf, oneOf, allOf (combinators; the parser collapses them onto the first branch that carries structure); description and title (kept as slot description). Things the parser does not model: external $ref URLs, patternProperties, additionalProperties, if/then/else, and the full semantics of allOf merging.

cards.q: How does the schema flattener work?
cards.easy: It walks each schema recursively and emits one record per leaf field, with a dotted path, a type, whether it is required, and whether it sits inside an array. Containers are not slots; only their leaves are.
cards.deep: extract.flattenSchema(root) calls visit(node, path, name, required, repeated, depth). If depth exceeds MAX_DEPTH = 7 it stops. A $ref is resolved against the root (local #/ refs only) and added to activeRefs for the current branch, so a recursive schema visits each ref at most once per branch. anyOf, oneOf or allOf collapse onto the first branch with properties, items or a $ref. An object recurses into each property with path parent.key and required = parent_required AND key in required. An array of objects recurses with path + '[]' and repeated = true; an array of scalars is itself a slot. Leaves produce a Slot {path, name, type, required, description, enumValues, hasDefault, repeated}. coreFieldPath strips envelope keys (data, response_data, result, items, records) and [] markers so data.items[].id compares like id. normalizeTool decides hasOutputSchema by ignoring status leaves such as successful, error and log_id; an envelope with nothing else is not a real output shape. Cost is linear in schema nodes, bounded by depth 7.

cards.q: What was the requiredness bug?
cards.easy: Fields inside an optional attachment object were reported as required input, so the reply tool appeared to demand an attachment file key from the user. The fix was to treat a field as required only if every level above it is also required.
cards.deep: JSON Schema's required list is local to its object: attachment.s3key may be required within attachment while attachment itself is optional, in which case the caller owes nothing. The first version took requiredness from the leaf's own parent only. The fix in visit() passes required && requiredKeys.has(key) down the recursion, so requiredness compounds along the path. The check.py assertion 'fields inside the optional attachment are not required input' verifies that no askUser entry for GOOGLESUPER_REPLY_TO_THREAD starts with s3key or mimetype; in the committed graph attachment.s3key and attachment.mimetype are both required: false. It is one of the four bugs found only because an assertion was written for a case decided in advance.

cards.q: What are the failure modes of the flattener, and how would you harden it?
cards.easy: It takes shortcuts: it follows only the first meaningful branch of an either/or schema, it stops at seven levels deep, and it only follows references inside the same document. Each shortcut can hide a field a tool really returns.
cards.deep: (1) Combinator collapse: anyOf and oneOf are unions, so taking the first structural branch drops fields that exist only in other branches; allOf should merge all branches, not pick one. Fix: visit every branch and union the slots, marking branch provenance. (2) MAX_DEPTH = 7 can truncate deep payloads (for example nested message parts), producing false negatives for handles that sit deep. (3) Only local refs (#/...) are resolved; a remote $ref leaves the node unresolved. (4) The activeRefs guard visits each recursive ref once per branch, which is correct for termination but means a self similar structure contributes one level only. (5) Arrays of tuples use items[0] only. (6) additionalProperties and patternProperties are ignored, so map shaped outputs keyed by id are invisible. cards.q: Why doesn't simple name matching between inputs and outputs work?
cards.easy: Matching input names to output names and drawing an edge takes twenty lines and fails at catalog scale for three reasons: common names like id, name and query collide across unrelated tools; a bare id means nothing without its parent field; and almost every response embeds other objects, so nearly every tool looks like it produces everything.
cards.deep: (1) Collisions: id, name, query, type, path and state appear on hundreds of unrelated tools, so name matching wires a mail client to a source control API. Fix: resolve every handle to a namespaced entity, scoped to the owning service. (2) Bare ids: the most common real shape is data.threads[].id; the leaf is id and the meaning is in the parent segment, so discarding the path hides the thread listing, the most important producer in the catalog. Fix: three tier resolution (leaf, nearest meaningful ancestor, the tool's own object). (3) Embedded objects: a workflow run response contains a full repository, so CANCEL_WORKFLOW_RUN literally 'produces' a repository name. Fix: split producers into primary and incidental by the head noun of the tool's object phrase and suppress incidental ones when a primary exists.

cards.q: How is each input slot classified?
cards.easy: Every input lands in one of five buckets: can be supplied by another tool, written by the user, a paging or formatting knob, a fixed list of options, or looks like a handle but no entity covers it yet. The last bucket is reported, not hidden.

cards.q: What are primary and incidental producers, and why does the head noun matter?
cards.easy: A primary producer is a tool whose purpose is to give you that thing, like a repository listing giving repository names. An incidental producer happens to include it, like a workflow run response that embeds a whole repository. The tool's name decides which: the last noun of its object phrase says what it is about.
cards.deep: graph.ts marks a produced entity primary when slugImpliesProduction(slug, entity) holds. verbAndObject tokenises the slug on underscores, finds the first verb in LIST, SEARCH, GET, FETCH, FIND (read) or CREATE, and takes the object phrase: tokens after the verb up to the first preposition (FOR, TO, IN, OF, FROM, BY, WITH, ON, AS, AT, INTO, USING), dropping articles (A, AN, THE, ALL, MY). headMatches checks the last token of the phrase against the entity's object nouns, then the whole phrase joined, then the last two tokens joined (PULL_REQUEST). English compounds are head final: CREATE_A_REPOSITORY_VARIABLE has head VARIABLE and yields no repo; CREATE_AN_ORGANIZATION_REPOSITORY has head REPOSITORY and yields one; CREATE_AN_ISSUE_COMMENT has head COMMENT and yields a comment, not an issue. Matching any token in the phrase gets all three wrong. In plans, incidental producers are dropped whenever a primary one exists.

cards.q: Write down the producer score.
cards.easy: Each candidate producer gets points for coming from a real output schema, being in the same service and toolkit, being a primary producer, being a read tool, and having the entity as its head noun; it loses points for burying the field deep in the response and for having a long, specific name.
cards.deep: producerScore(slug, entity, via, depth, primary, sameService, sameToolkit) = 50[via = schema] + 70[sameService] + 30[sameToolkit] + 100[primary] + 30[read verb] + 40[head noun hit] - 12 max(0, depth - 1) - min(24, 2 x tokens(slug)) + 8[slug contains _LIST_] + 6[slug contains _SEARCH_]. Depth counts segments of the envelope stripped path, so a repo name at data.items[].name (depth 2) beats one at data.repository.owner.login (depth 3). The token penalty prefers general tools (LIST_REPOSITORIES) over narrow ones. Candidates are sorted by score descending, ties broken alphabetically by slug for determinism, and capped at PRECURSOR_CAP = 12. Weights were set by hand to make the fixture cases and the assertions come out right; there is no fitted model and no labelled ranking data, so the weights are a heuristic.

cards.q: How is the per tool plan built?
cards.easy: For each input the tool needs, the code finds every tool that can produce it, keeps the purpose built ones, prefers ones in the same toolkit, ranks them, and keeps the top 12. Required inputs that nothing can produce, or that the user must write, go on an 'ask the user' list.
cards.deep: For each slot with an entityId: candidates = producersOf(entity) excluding the tool itself (which removes self loops); if any candidate is primary, keep only primaries; if any is in the same toolkit, keep only those; score, sort and cap at 12. If a required entity slot has no candidates, push 'name (entity, no producer found)' to askUser. Required slots classified user_supplied or unresolved are pushed to askUser too; control and enum slots never are. cards.q: Why is the graph bipartite?
cards.easy: If you drew an arrow from every tool that produces a repository owner to every tool that needs one, that one entity alone would create tens of thousands of arrows. Making the entities themselves nodes means each tool connects once to each entity, and the path tool, entity, tool reads as 'run this before that'.
cards.deep: Direct encoding: edges = sum over entities of producers x consumers. github.repo_owner has 146 producers and 637 consumers in the committed graph, so it alone would contribute about 93,000 tool to tool edges. Bipartite encoding: tools and entities are both nodes; produces edges go tool to entity, requires edges go entity to tool, so edges = sum of producers + consumers, 3,278 in total. The hub structure becomes legible (repo_owner, repo_name, user_login and email are the hubs), and a two hop path LIST_THREADS to gmail.thread_id to REPLY_TO_THREAD is exactly the ordering answer. It is the same idea as factoring a dense bipartite projection, or as a Petri net with places (entities) and transitions (tools). The requires edges also carry required true or false, so the viewer can filter to hard dependencies.

cards.q: Define bipartite graph, hub, degree, two hop path, and opaque handle as used here.
cards.easy: A bipartite graph has two kinds of nodes, and edges only connect one kind to the other. A hub is a node with many connections; degree is the number of connections. A two hop path goes tool, then entity, then tool. An opaque handle is a value a person cannot reasonably make up.
cards.deep: Bipartite: node set split into tools T and entities E, with every edge between T and E; here directed (T to E is produces, E to T is requires). Degree of an entity = producerCount + consumerCount, which sizes entity nodes in the viewer (mapData(deg, 0, 120, 22, 62)). Hub: high degree entity; github.repo_owner (146 producers, 637 consumers) dominates GitHub. Two hop path: t1 to e to t2 means t1 can supply an argument t2 needs; it is the immediate predecessor relation, not a full plan. Opaque handle: Entity.opaque = true (thread id, issue number, commit sha); semi opaque: opaque = false but often fetched (email address, repo owner, branch). Slot buckets: tool_derived, user_supplied, control, enum_or_constant, unresolved. Primary producer: slug head noun names the entity; incidental: any other tool whose output embeds it.

cards.q: How would you turn this into a call order? Explain topological sorting and whether it applies.
cards.easy: A topological sort lists the steps of a dependency graph so that every step comes after the steps it depends on. This project does not build full plans yet; it answers 'what comes immediately before', and turning that into an order needs a slightly different algorithm because a tool needs all of its inputs but each input can come from any one of several tools.
cards.deep: Kahn's algorithm: compute in degrees, queue nodes with in degree 0, repeatedly pop a node, append it, decrement its successors' in degrees, and enqueue any that reach 0; O(V + E). If nodes remain when the queue empties, the graph has a cycle. DFS alternative: reverse postorder. Neither applies directly here because the graph is an AND/OR graph: a tool fires only when ALL its required entities are available (AND), and an entity is available when ANY producer has fired or the user supplied it (OR). A plain topological sort would demand every producer, which is wrong. The right tool is forward chaining to a fixpoint: start from entities the user knows, mark a tool runnable when its count of unmet required entities reaches 0, mark its outputs available, repeat. With counters this runs in linear time, the same method as Horn clause satisfiability. Backward chaining from the goal tool, picking the best scored producer per missing entity with a visited set, gives a concrete plan. README: no transitive planning is built.
evidence: repo:tool-dependency-graph/README.md: - **No transitive planning.** This answers "what comes immediately before".

cards.q: Does the graph have cycles, and how would a planner handle them?
cards.easy: Yes. A tool like 'get a repository' needs the owner and name and also returns them, so it both consumes and produces the same entity. The current plan builder simply never suggests a tool as its own prerequisite; a full planner would treat already known values as satisfied and refuse to revisit anything on the current path.
cards.deep: Cycles arise in three ways: self loops (GET_A_REPOSITORY requires and produces repo_owner), mutual loops (an issue listing needs repo_owner, and some repository tools return issue data), and hub loops through repo_owner and user_login. The plan builder filters candidates with p.slug !== tool.slug, which removes self loops from precursor lists, and it only answers one hop, so it never loops. For transitive planning: (1) forward chaining to a fixpoint is cycle safe by construction, because each entity flips from unavailable to available once and each tool fires once, so it terminates in O(V + E); (2) backward chaining needs a visited set on the current path, and a cycle means that branch is unsatisfiable unless something on it is user known; (3) a cost aware version (shortest hyperpath, Knuth's generalisation of Dijkstra to AND/OR graphs) picks the cheapest derivation and handles cycles because costs only grow. Practical rule: treat non opaque entities (owner, repo, branch) as user known by default, which breaks most GitHub cycles.

cards.q: What is the time and space complexity of the pipeline?
cards.easy: Everything is close to linear in the size of the catalog, so the full 1,391 tool build is quick. The slowest parts are matching each field against all 46 entities and comparing each consumer with all producers of its entities.
cards.deep: Let T tools, S total slots (7,101 inputs plus outputs), E entities (46), A aliases per entity. Flattening: O(schema nodes), bounded by depth 7. Service inference: O(T x markers). resolveEntity: O(E x A) per slot, so O(S x E x A); a hash map from alias to entity would make it O(S). Output resolution adds a walk over path segments, O(depth) per slot. Edges: O(slots), giving 3,278. Plans: for each consumer slot, O(p log p) over that entity's producers p (repo_owner has 146), so O(sum over consumer slots of p log p), about the size of the direct projection only in the worst case, then capped at 12. Space: O(T + S + edges). The direct tool to tool graph would be O(sum of producers x consumers), more than 93,000 edges from repo_owner alone, which is why the bipartite form matters for storage and display as well as legibility. The viewer caps each service view at 260 nodes for the same reason.

cards.q: How does the visualization work?
cards.easy: Opening graph.html in a browser shows the graph for one service at a time, with entities as large nodes and tools as small ones. Clicking a tool shows what it needs and what can supply it. It works offline from a double click, with no server.
cards.deep: viz.ts reads data/graph.json, keeps only the fields the page reads (roughly halving the payload), escapes '</' so the data cannot close the script tag, and inlines it into viz.template.html as graph.html. Inlining avoids a fetch, which file:// pages cannot do because of CORS. The page uses a vendored Cytoscape.js with the cose force directed layout (nodeRepulsion 9000, idealEdgeLength 70, 900 iterations). The view is scoped to one service with options to show only opaque entities or only required edges; tools are ranked by degree and capped at 260, with a visible note saying how many of how many are shown. Entity node size maps degree. Produces and requires edges have different colours. The header states the stats line, including how many required typed inputs another tool can supply.

cards.q: Why do this statically instead of letting the LLM work out the order from tool descriptions?
cards.easy: A model can often guess that a reply needs a thread ID, but it has to work that out again on every call, it can make up IDs, and its guesses cannot be audited. A precomputed graph is deterministic, cheap to look up, and every edge points to the schema field that justifies it.
cards.deep: Static graph: deterministic, inspectable provenance (every produces edge cites an output path such as threads.id), zero tokens at runtime, testable with assertions, and usable for tool retrieval (pull a tool's precursors into context). Its limits: only as good as the schemas, heuristics for ranking, no runtime context (whether the user already gave an address). LLM only: handles novel phrasing and context, but costs tokens per decision, is nondeterministic, cannot see output schemas unless they are in context (often too large for 1,391 tools), and fails silently by fabricating handles. Runtime tracing (mining successful agent trajectories for call sequences) learns real usage but needs traffic and inherits the agent's mistakes. The complementary design: the static graph proposes candidates and constraints, the model decides among them with runtime context, and traces validate and reweight edges.

cards.q: Why a hand built registry and rule based matching instead of embeddings or an LLM labeller?
cards.easy: Rules are slower to extend but every decision can be explained and tested, and the project's priority was that no wrong edge gets in silently. Anything uncertain is left unresolved and reported instead of guessed.
cards.deep: Embedding similarity between field names would catch spellings the aliases miss but would also reintroduce the collisions the registry exists to prevent (id, name, state embed close to everything) and give no crisp threshold. An LLM labeller could propose entities for the 568 unresolved slots quickly, but its labels need review, and its errors are not reproducible. The registry costs: 46 entities written by hand, alias lists that need upkeep, and coverage limited to what was anticipated. The design choice is explicit in entities.ts: anything still ambiguous is left unmapped and reported rather than guessed, and google_other parks low confidence tools. A pragmatic hybrid: use an LLM to propose new entities and aliases from the unresolved bucket, then review and commit them as rules with a test each.

cards.q: How are names normalised before matching?
cards.easy: Field names come in many spellings (threadId, thread_id, ThreadID), so each one is converted to lower case snake_case, and singular and plural forms are both tried, before comparing with the registry.
cards.deep: normalizeName: insert an underscore between a lowercase letter or digit and an uppercase letter (threadId to thread_Id), lowercase, replace runs of non alphanumerics with one underscore, trim leading and trailing underscores. nameVariants adds the singular when the name ends in s and always adds a plural, so label_ids matches alias label_id. segmentNames applies the same singular and plural logic to path segments against object nouns. coreFieldPath strips envelope keys and [] markers before computing depth. Failure modes: naive pluralisation (status to statu, address to addresse are harmless misses; irregular plurals such as people and person are listed explicitly in objectNouns); abbreviations (repo against repository) need explicit aliases; and a name like 'issue' is both an alias of issue_number and a common word, which scoping to github limits.

cards.q: What is the tech stack and how do you run it?
cards.easy: TypeScript run directly by Bun, with no build step, a Python script for the checks, and a single HTML page for the viewer. With no catalog of your own it runs on an 8 tool sample.
cards.deep: bun install; bun run src/graph.ts builds the graph (data/catalog/*.json if present, else data/sample/catalog.json, writing data/graph.sample.json so a full build is never overwritten); bun run src/viz.ts rebuilds graph.html; python3 check.py verifies, against data/graph.json or the sample build. Layout: src/extract.ts (schema flattening, knows nothing about any service), src/entities.ts (registry, service inference, producer ranking), src/graph.ts (bipartite graph, plans, stats), src/viz.ts (inlining), check.py (eight assertions), viz.template.html. Separation of concerns is deliberate: the schema walker is generic so the domain rules stay readable and swappable. Outputs: graph.json with generatedAt, stats, entities (with producer and consumer counts), tools (slots and produces with evidence), edges, plans.

cards.q: What are the limitations?
cards.easy: The entity list is hand built and incomplete, producer ranking is a heuristic, the graph trusts schemas that are sometimes thinner than the real API, it only answers 'what comes immediately before', and there is no measured precision or recall.
cards.deep: From the README: 46 entities cover common handles, and 568 handle shaped slots still resolve to nothing; producer ranking prefers a read verb with the entity as direct object, shallow paths, and locality, which gets common cases right and exotic ones wrong; a contacts search tool declares no email in its output; no transitive planning; the raw catalog is not redistributed. Additional limits found while preparing this deck: the precursor list for github.repo_name contains incidental tools because repository listings call the field name; github.issue_id has zero producers, likely because tier 2 takes the first registry match; 112 Google tools are parked in google_other with no service; 153 tools have no informative output schema; and the eight assertions are a spot check, not an eval set.

cards.q: What breaks at 10x and 100x the catalog size, and what would production need?
cards.easy: At ten times the tools the hand written registry becomes the bottleneck, name collisions multiply across many more services, and the heuristics for ranking producers get more wrong cases. Production would need semi automatic entity discovery, a labelled evaluation, schema version tracking, and feedback from real agent runs.
cards.deep: 10x (about 14,000 tools, dozens of toolkits): registry upkeep scales with services, so entities must be proposed automatically (cluster handle shaped unresolved slots by name and parent segment, LLM proposes, human approves). Service inference by regex markers per service does not scale; toolkit metadata or learned classifiers are needed. Matching cost O(S x E x A) needs an alias hash index. 100x: cross toolkit entities (email, URL, user id across many SaaS products) need identity mapping between namespaces; producer lists per hub entity grow, so ranking needs learned weights from usage traces; incremental rebuilds on schema change with diffing and versioned graphs; a serving layer (precursor lookup API, cached plans). Quality: a labelled set with precision@k per service, regression assertions per bug, and monitoring of agent failures attributable to missing precursors.

cards.q: What would you do next?
cards.easy: Build the planner that chains one hop answers into a full call order, build a small labelled set to measure precision and recall, and use the unresolved list plus real agent runs to grow the registry.
cards.deep: (1) Transitive planner: forward chaining from user known entities to a fixpoint, then backward extraction of the cheapest derivation using producer scores as costs, cycle safe. (2) Evaluation: about 100 hand labelled consumer tools, precision@1 and @3 and recall, per service; add every found error as an assertion. (3) Fix the observed resolver issues: name under repositories[] to repo_name, issue global id vs number disambiguation by preferring exact aliases over first match, and suppressing precursor lists with no primary producer. (4) Registry growth from the 568 unresolved slots with LLM proposals reviewed by hand. (5) Union over anyOf and oneOf branches in the flattener. (6) Validate edges against real agent traces and reweight producerScore from observed success.

cards.q: 99.9% coverage sounds like a vanity number.

cards.deep: Concede: the denominator is 1,770 resolved slots, not 2,728 required ones; 'has a producer' says nothing about whether the top suggestion is correct; and the repo_name precursor list shows that a slot can count as covered while its suggestions are poor. Defend: the number is reported with its denominator, the 568 unresolved handles are published rather than hidden, every produces edge cites a declared output field (the slug fallback fired zero times), and the two uncovered slots are named. What would make it a real metric: precision@k on a labelled sample.

The honest figure is that 65% of required inputs are typed handles, and almost all of those have a producer. It also doesn't measure whether the top suggestion is right. That needs a labelled set, which I haven't built yet.

cards.q: Modern models figure out tool order on their own. Why build this?
cards.easy: Models often guess right on small toolsets, but on 1,391 tools the schemas do not fit in context, the guesses cost tokens on every call, and a wrong guess shows up as a made up ID. The graph gives the model a checked shortlist instead of asking it to rediscover the structure.
cards.deep: Concede: with a handful of tools and clear descriptions, a strong model rarely needs this, and the graph has no runtime context. Defend: output schemas are what reveal producers, and they are large; 1,391 tools cannot all be in context; tool retrieval benefits from pulling precursors along with the chosen tool; the graph is deterministic and auditable, which matters when an agent acts on a user's mail or repos; and a fabricated id fails late and confusingly. The intended use is complementary: graph proposes, model decides.
cards.say: On a small toolset, sure, the model usually gets it. At 1,391 tools the output schemas don't fit in context, and output schemas are what tell you who produces a handle. The graph hands the model a short, checked list of precursors. The model still makes the runtime call.

cards.q: A registry of 46 hand written entities doesn't scale.
cards.easy: It does not scale by hand, agreed. The design makes the gap visible: 568 handle shaped inputs are reported as unresolved, and that list is exactly where new entities came from. The next step is to have a model propose entities from that list and keep a human in the approval step.
cards.deep: Concede: adding a toolkit means writing entities and aliases, and coverage is 65% of required inputs. Defend: hand built rules mean every edge is explainable and testable; the unresolved bucket turns coverage gaps into a prioritised backlog (it produced repository_id, project_id, runner_id and invitation_id); and the generic parts (schema walker, three tier resolution, head noun ranking, bipartite graph) carry over unchanged. Scale path: cluster unresolved slots by name and parent, have an LLM draft entities, review and commit each with an assertion.
cards.say: By hand, no, and I'd say that first. What scales is the loop. Anything handle shaped that doesn't resolve gets reported, and that list is where several entities came from. I'd have a model draft new entities from it and review each one with a test.

cards.q: Your producer score is a pile of hand tuned magic numbers.
cards.easy: Fair. The weights were set by hand, and there is no labelled ranking data to fit them. They do encode a clear ordering of priorities, though: locality first, then purpose, then shallowness, and the assertions check the cases that matter most.
cards.deep: Concede: +100 primary, +70 same service, +50 schema, +40 head hit, +30 read verb, -12 per depth level and the rest are not learned, not validated beyond eight assertions, and their interactions are not analysed; small changes can reorder long lists. Defend: the weights implement a lexicographic intent (a primary local producer from a real schema should beat anything else), the tie break is deterministic, and two hard filters (primary only when any primary exists, local toolkit only when any local exists) do most of the work before scoring. Improvement: collect accepted and rejected suggestions from labelling or agent traces and fit a pairwise ranking model (logistic regression on the same features), keeping the features interpretable.
cards.say: Fair hit. They're hand set, and I don't have labelled ranking data to fit them yet. They encode an order I can defend: local beats remote, purpose built beats incidental, shallow beats buried. Most of the work is done by two hard filters before the score even runs. With labels, I'd fit a simple pairwise ranker on the same features.

cards.q: Parsing English out of tool slugs is brittle. What happens with slugs that don't follow your pattern?
cards.easy: It is brittle at the edges, and it is used narrowly: only to decide whether a producer is primary and, in a fallback that never fired, to guess outputs. When the slug pattern fails, the tool is treated as incidental rather than wrong.
cards.deep: Concede: verbs outside LIST, SEARCH, GET, FETCH, FIND and CREATE are ignored; head first slugs (REPOSITORY_LIST) or nominalised verbs would not parse; prepositions outside the list would let modifiers leak into the object phrase. Defend: these catalogs use a consistent VERB_ARTICLE_OBJECT_PREP pattern, so the heuristic covers the common case; a parse failure demotes a producer from primary to incidental, which only matters when no primary producer exists; and edges themselves come from output schemas, never from slugs, because the fallback fired zero times. Hardening: add verbs from a frequency count over all slugs, and test the parser on every slug in the catalog to list the ones it cannot parse.
cards.say: At the edges, yes. But the slug parse only decides primary versus incidental. The edges themselves come from output schemas, and the slug fallback never fired. If a slug doesn't parse, that tool gets demoted, not wired wrong.

cards.easy: Lead with the agent failure it prevents, then what was built, the honest headline, and how it was checked.
cards.deep: One sentence on the failure (a call needs a handle the agent cannot produce), one on the artifact (a dependency map built from 1,391 schemas), one on the result with its denominator, one on validation and what is next (a labelled eval and a planner).
cards.say: Agents often fail a tool call because it needs an ID they can't produce, like the thread they're replying to. I built a static analyser that reads 1,391 tool schemas and says which tools must run first and what to ask the user. Two thirds of required inputs turn out to be handles another tool can supply, and almost all of those have a producer. Next I'd add a labelled evaluation and a planner that chains the steps.

cards.q: Explain it to a staff engineer.
cards.easy: Give the three failures of name matching and the fix for each, the bipartite design, the numbers with denominators, and volunteer the weak spots.
cards.deep: Hit: namespaced, service scoped entities; three tier resolution for bare ids; head noun primary versus incidental; bipartite encoding (repo_owner 146 x 637 as the motivating hub); 1,768 of 1,770 with the 65% framing; zero slug inference; and the gaps: no labelled precision, repo_name precursor noise, issue_id first match, one hop only.

Bare ids resolve through their parent path, then the tool's own object. Producers are primary only if the slug's head noun names the entity. Tools and entities are both nodes, which keeps the edge count linear. Every edge cites a declared output field. The gaps are a missing labelled eval, some noisy precursor lists, and no multi step planner yet.

cards.q: Explain it to a product manager.
cards.easy: Frame it as a map that tells an assistant what to look up first and what to ask the customer, which cuts failed actions and pointless questions.
cards.deep: Use the email example: reply to a thread needs a thread from a listing; sending to 'Priya' needs a contacts lookup first; the subject and body come from the user. The PM value: fewer failed actions, fewer questions the user cannot answer, and a list of gaps to prioritise.
cards.say: It's a map for an AI assistant that uses lots of tools. Before it replies to an email thread, it needs the thread's ID, so it has to look the thread up first. If you say 'email Priya', it needs to find her address. The map tells the assistant what to look up first and what it should actually ask you. That means fewer failed actions and fewer questions you can't answer.
